entries.title: How Anthropic Redesigned Source Control
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at the architecture behind Scion.
entries.content:
A Pile of MCP Connectors Is Not a Context Engine (Sponsored)

Your team connected Slack, Jira and GitHub over MCP, and engineers still spend their time steering agents to the right answer. This article looks at why: connectors fetch from one tool at a time, so every agent stitches the pieces together itself, trusts the first doc that looks right, and adds a search to your token bill each time.

Read what changes when a context engine sits on top of your connectors: the same coding task finished 83% faster at 48% lower cost.

Anthropic has recently reached a point where coding isn’t the bottleneck for them. Claude is able to do a lot of heavy lifting. It can iterate on research loops. Or optimize complex programs. Or even build new services from scratch.

However, the main problem Anthropic faces is that the infrastructure they have around writing code is not able to keep up with the amount of code being generated by its agents. Activities like downloading repositories, preparing workspaces, and recording changes are becoming major bottlenecks.

To solve this problem, the Anthropic engineering team built Scion. You can think of Scion as a source control system that has been designed around a huge repository and clients that are almost always online. In this article, we’ll look at the architecture behind Scion. Here’s what we will cover:

  • How source control works

  • Anthropic’s problem with source control

  • Why Git couldn’t solve the problem

  • How Scion works

  • How changes are handled in Scion

  • How Scion caches data

  • How Anthropic scales Scion

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

How Source Control Works

As you will already know, a software project is made up of files that change continuously. Developers add features. They correct mistakes and update dependencies. They also sometimes need to recover an earlier version. A source control system records all these changes and lets multiple developers work on the same codebase.

Let’s look at a few key terms related to source control.

A repository contains the project’s versioned information. Next, you have a commit that denotes a specific version along with other details such as the author, a description, and a history of the earlier commits.

A branch is used to demarcate a line of development. For example, your main branch signifies the line of code into which you integrate all the reviewed and approved changes. Different developers can work on different branches and combine their code through a merge process.

The files present on a developer’s machine are known as the working copy. A checkout process prepares those files for a specific version.

Lastly, you also have automated systems that rely on source control. Continuous integration (CI) runs processes such as compilation, testing, and other checks when code changes. Each job may need a workspace that contains the appropriate version of the code. Coding agents and research jobs need similar environments.

Anthropic’s Problem with Source Control

Anthropic stores a large amount of its code in a monorepo. You can think of a monorepo as a shared repository that contains multiple projects and components. This way, code that is related can share a common history. But it also means that many separate activities might depend on the same source control infrastructure.

But a large repository is only a part of the story. Anthropic’s problem is much deeper. They report that merged changes have grown from roughly 2500 per day in May 2026 to more than 30000 per day by September. Meanwhile, the size of its main branch’s history is close to 100 GB. Even a compressed working copy goes beyond 25 GB.

The CI system is doing approximately 25 million checkouts per day. This number is before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. To be clear, you shouldn’t think of these checkouts as individual code changes. A single change can spawn many jobs. And each job prepares an environment for doing its work. Ultimately, your infrastructure workload can get much larger than the number of changes being merged.

For example, a naive approach to transfer a compressed working copy for every CI checkout can generate more than 600 PB of traffic per day. Therefore, the practical problem Anthropic faces has two sides. One is that the system must be able to accept new changes quickly. Second, it must be able to distribute the code to a huge number of consumers. If you improve only one aspect, the other can become a bottleneck.

Why Git Couldn’t Solve the Problem

The local independence of Git becomes quite expensive in this type of workload. As you might know, Git is designed in a way that an ordinary full clone of the codebase can be used as a self-contained repository.

When the necessary data is locally available, you can use Git to inspect history, compare versions, and create commits without the need to contact a central service. This is a great strength of Git.

However, Anthropic’s workload is such that this independence is not valuable. Most of the clients are automated jobs and agents that already depend on network services. At the same time, if you give those clients a good chunk of repository data, it leads to repeated transfer, storage, and maintenance costs.

To be clear, Git also has ways to reduce those costs. Anthropic used a bunch of these strategies. For example, they use features like shallow clones, sparse checkouts, partial clones, internal mirrors, and repository seeds. Each of these techniques can handle different parts of the problem. For example, a feature like sparse checkout helps deal with files that are part of the workspace.

The first architecture Anthropic built was around the use of Git. You had jobs start from seeds, obtain additional data through caches, and use layers of repository mirrors. At its peak, the Anthropic engineering team was operating several hundred internal mirrors to distribute traffic. But they had to keep all these mirrors in sync with each other as the repository data changed. Seeds also became outdated as the rate of merging increased. Operations that needed historical data became a lot harder to manage because clients held only partial repository data.

The Anthropic team realized that its workflow already had one authoritative shared repository while the infrastructure supported a lot of independence at the client level. With Scion, they changed this responsibility allocation approach.

How Scion Works

Scion makes the server responsible for repository operations. It assumes that clients can reach a source control service when they need data.

In this setup, the server answers historical data queries, calculates diffs, and creates commits. It also performs merges and rebases. The client (known as scn) maintains a limited cache and prepares files on disk. It watches for local filesystem changes and provides an interface for developers and jobs to deal with the service.

This setup is known as the client-server asymmetry. You can think of it as the client and server having different capabilities and responsibilities. For example, let’s say you have a tool that needs to find out the change behind a particular line of code. This operation is commonly known as blame. In Scion’s operating model, the tool asks the service for the answer to its question. It doesn’t need to assemble enough local history to calculate the answer.

The same principle applies when you’ve to create changes. In Git, you have a commit that’s created locally and later shared through a push. In Scion, you create a commit using a server operation. There’s no separate push step.

You might think that such a centralized service uses a single server that contains everything. But that’s not the case. Anthropic distributes the data and scales the service across machines. There’s no fully materialized repository on any single individual server. The tradeoff is that you have a strong dependence on service availability and connectivity.

How Changes are Handled by Scion

Changesets provide a small, durable record of each change. Once you create a commit on the server, you need to ensure that they are accepted efficiently.

Scion’s basic unit for managing this is a changeset. You can think of this changeset as a durable record of a change. You can easily construct other useful representations of the repository from this changeset.

To understand its structure, two terms are important. First is a blob that stores the contents of the file. Second is a tree that describes the contents of the directory. It connects names to files and subdirectories. In Git, a commit points to a root tree that represents the project at that version.

A Scion changeset records the files that changed relative to its first parent. This happens together with a reference to their contents. For example, let’s say you have a change that updates a file named “docs/guide[dot]md”, deletes “src/legacy[dot]rs, and modifies “tools/build[dot]sh”. The changeset keeps a record of those file changes and their relevant references. It also keeps the parent information and author details. Here, “changed files” doesn’t mean a sequence of line-by-line patches.

A merge can also have multiple parents. The first parent gives you the baseline against which Scion records its file changes.

Changeset metadata is stored in Spanner, which is a distributed database. Compressed file contents are kept in cloud object storage. The root tree is derived by the server rather than being stored directly inside the changeset.

This way, you can record a change based on the changed data and affected structures. No need to process the whole repository.

How Scion Caches Data

Using immutable objects makes it easy to use shared caching.

Scion recognizes its source control objects by their contents. This technique is known as content-addressing. In this approach, you have a hash function that calculates an identifier from the contents of an object. The system can then find that object later using this identifier. If there’s a change in the content, the new object gets a different ID value.

This way, your stored objects are immutable. A specific ID continues to refer to the same data. For example, let’s say you have a cache that contains a particular version of “parser[dot].rs”. If you have another job that asks for the same object, the cache can return it without asking another server if the contents have been modified. If there’s a new version of the file, it means the object is different.

There are two consequences of this. One is that you can use identical content. Cached historical objects don’t need freshness checks merely because development is happening somewhere else in the repository.

Git uses content addressing. But the way Scion differs is in how extensively its service and architecture are organized around asking for and caching these objects.

Information still changes in the system. For example, let’s say the name “main” moves as changes are integrated. The immutable object that represents a specific version and the mutable name that identifies the latest version require you to treat things differently.

How Anthropic Scales Scion

Scion scales by combining shared source control APIs with a hierarchy of caches. Its design is such that answering questions is separate from delivering the files needed for a working directory.

The first point is that repository operations move into a shared service. Many tools need information such as which changes affected a file, who modified a line, and so on. If you’ve to maintain a local repository to answer such questions, it creates a lot of downloading and maintenance work.

Scion exposes these operations through APIs. You can have clients ask the servers directly. The servers can compute derived data when needed and save those results to Spanner. With this, any jobs that only need these answers don’t have to prepare a local repository.

Second, you have immutable objects that make caching pretty simple. As we saw earlier, Scion identifies objects using hashes based on their contents. An existing ID always refers to the same data.

Third, clients only request the objects they need. Scion represents directory structure through trees and file contents through blobs. The client identifies what is missing. So the server receives explicit object requests rather than having to think about a customized transfer.

Fourth, by sharing caches, they reduce the need for repeated downloads and computation. On a compute node, jobs talk to “scion-daemon”. You can think of it as a background process that shares cached objects across jobs.

Any missing objects come from “scion-cache”. This is the regional caching layer that’s shared across many nodes. If that layer also misses, you can get the data from authoritative Scion servers that read from Spanner or cloud storage.

Lastly, you also have strict cache boundaries that help contain failures. All three layers support the same object-request interface. Otherwise, a regional cache that fails could cause its consumers to overwhelm the authoritative servers.

Conclusion

The Anthropic engineering team learnt a lot of important lessons while building and running Scion.

First was that rapid development is very possible with a small team. For reference, it was just a team of seven people that built both Scion and Antique (which is their code review tool).

The second takeaway was that developers are still valuable, but their scope of work is changing. All of the developers working on this system would rate Claude as better at writing code than they are. But the developers were critical in providing invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and considering the trade-offs in the design decisions. A lot of the developer work revolved around stopping Claude from taking a certain path.

Third, they were able to make things more optimized and also deliver high-quality stuff. Due to Claude’s ability to write a ton of code much faster than human developers, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases they’ve ever created.

Fourth, they were able to achieve a new level of operational excellence. The team uses Claude Tag heavily so that they can monitor each component of the system.

entries.title: How Netflix Uses AI Agents for Performance Engineering
entries.summary: The Netflix engineering team has developed an autonomous performance agent system. In this article, we’ll be learning more about it.
entries.content:
The real benefits of end-to-end observability (Sponsored)

How does full-stack observability impact engineering speed, incident response, and cost control?

In this eBook from Datadog, you’ll learn how real teams across industries are using observability to:

  • Reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR)

  • Cut tooling costs and improve team efficiency

  • Align business and engineering KPIs

See how unifying your stack leads to faster troubleshooting and long-term operational gains.

Performance engineering is the discipline in which you design, analyze, and optimize software systems so that they run quickly. Also, they should use resources efficiently. In distributed architectures, the focus of any performance engineering activity is on shaving milliseconds off response times. Or locating execution bottlenecks in CPU or memory. Or making sure infrastructure costs are kept under control.

Historically, performance engineering work has been slow. And manual. You often depend on a small group of really skilled developers. However, with the rise of AI-assisted software development, there’s a contradiction. Developers can write and ship code faster than ever. No matter what their skill level may be. But that code often introduces subtle performance problems.

To solve this problem, the Netflix engineering team has developed an autonomous performance agent system. In this article, we’ll be learning more about it. Here’s what we will cover:

  • Bottlenecks for traditional performance work

  • The problem with AI-Generated code

  • Can LLMs handle profile data

  • The agentic profiling pipeline

  • The problems Netflix found in production

  • Safety, verification, and trust architecture

  • Shifting left

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

Bottlenecks For Traditional Performance Work

Traditional performance engineering work at Netflix was built on a highly iterative loop that is pretty much manual in nature.

First, you trigger profiling for an application. A developer tries to detect high latency or increased resource usage by triggering a profiler on a live production server.

In the second step, the profiler outputs raw trace data or flame graphs. The developer downloads these details to their local machine.

Third, the developer spends time looking at complex, color-coded flame graphs. They try to spot wide stack frames that might show signs of higher-than-normal CPU or memory consumption.

Next, the developer goes through the codebase looking for cryptic method names found in the flame graph. They try to make sense of the surrounding application logic to figure things out.

Fifth, the developer traces the execution path and identifies the inefficient operation. They write a proposed patch to fix the operation.

Moving further, the developers deploy the patch to an environment where any change in performance levels can be measured.

At the end, when new code paths are deployed in production, the developer starts the manual process once again.

As you may have noticed, this workflow doesn’t scale. Everything depends on a few domain experts who have a deep sense of understanding about low-level execution stacks. Since human attention is a scarce resource, you can investigate performance issues only for major incidents or obvious system slowdowns. Smaller but steady resource drains go unnoticed.

Why Braintrust, Raycast and Jane Street use WarpBuild (Sponsored)

Fast-moving teams ship more code than ever, and AI tools add even more. Their CI has to keep up without the bill getting out of hand.

That is why teams at Braintrust, Raycast, OpenRouter, Comcast and Jane Street run GitHub Actions on WarpBuild:

  • Twice as fast at half the cost

  • Linux, macOS and Windows on x86-64 and ARM64

  • Unlimited macOS concurrency

  • One line change to runs-on

Use code START50 for $50 in free credits.

The Problem with AI Code

The use of AI coding assistants has increased performance problems. There are two main reasons for this. The speed trap and the context gap.

Developers who are using AI tools can generate and ship code up to 10 times faster than before. No matter their skill level or knowledge of the system. But you cannot guarantee that code that is fast to generate also performs well. While your average developer might be able to write 10K lines of code in a few minutes, the team might have to spend years debugging regressions. Or dealing with code bloat. Or handling other architecture-related problems.

Also, if you’ve noticed, LLMs are great at syntax and local-level logic. If you ask an LLM to write a function or an API endpoint, it writes code that compiles successfully and runs without any obvious errors. It might also pass standard unit tests. However, the LLM has no idea about the host platform’s runtime environment.

For example, you can’t expect the LLM to know that a particular utility function being used in your code might run 10 million times per second on a critical request path. It cannot see the overall call stack. Neither can it understand memory allocation challenges that might exist inside a container running at peak load within your platform. Therefore, the code you write might appear good enough in isolation. But it can still waste a huge amount of resources when you run it at scale.

Can LLMs Handle Profile Data

Netflix wanted to test whether automation could remove these issues. They set up an experiment to find out if an LLM can read and make sense of raw profiling data directly.

Different languages have different profilers. But they use a shared language and store the same core information. For example, JVM’s async-profiler or Java Flight Recorder operates at 100 Hz sampling to capture execution traces, memory allocation rates, and thread lock contention. Python’s py-spy provides low-overhead, async stack sampling of live production processes. Go has pprof, which generates goroutine profiles, heap snapshots, and block contention data.

Each one of these profilers breaks down execution into call stacks. They track two main metrics. First, you have the inclusive time. This is the total time spent executing a function. It includes every child function and the subroutines called by this function. Second, you have the Self (CPU) Time. It’s the time spent running code purely inside the function itself. No external calls are involved.

With this exercise, the Netflix engineering team came to the conclusion that a single analytical pipeline could understand data from almost any programming runtime.

Another advantage of LLMs is that they don’t have to guess how an algorithm works from scratch. Since LLMs have been broadly trained on many software repositories, they are mostly familiar with classic programming anti-patterns. For example, they know that quadratic loops where a hot method is called again and again for each item in a collection aren’t a good idea. Also, loop invariants where you compute a calculation for every iteration of the loop instead of making the calculation once at the beginning. Other patterns include excessive object allocation on hot execution paths and “N+1” query patterns.

Due to this knowledge base of LLMs, you don’t need to ask an AI model to guess why an application might be performing poorly. You can build a workflow that asks the model to pattern-match known performance bugs against actual call stacks.

The Agentic Profiling Pipeline

Netflix built an automated performance system that wraps the LLM inside a well-defined pipeline.

A key lesson Netflix engineers learnt during this implementation was about scoping. If you feed an LLM a complete, raw stack trace without boundaries, it can get distracted. Often, the model spends a lot of reasoning tokens analyzing internal JVM garbage collection pauses, low-level Linux kernel syscalls, or even 3rd party open-source framework overhead.

Application developers don’t have any control over such internal library concerns or OS routines. Therefore, you need to provide the agent with strict package prefix rules. This way, the model can ignore generic platform noise and focus on tracing only the specific application code.

The Problems Netflix Found in Production

When the Netflix engineering team deployed the profiling pipeline against its production service, the agent found 4 major categories of performance bugs.

First was an algorithmic bottleneck that wasted 8.8% of CPU resources. The agent found an aggregation method using Java Streams where an immutable map was updated inside a reduction step.

      
// Anti-pattern: O(N^2) accumulation inside stream reduction
stream().reduce(ImmutableMap.of(), (acc, val) -> {
    return ImmutableMap.builder()
        .putAll(acc) // Copies every existing entry on every single step
        .put(val)
        .build();
});

Since putAll(acc) copies every existing key-value pair on every step, you need to copy elements again and again to build a map of size N. This results in quadratic complexity.

The agent modified the quadratic builder reduction with a linear collection approach.

      
// Optimized: O(N) single-pass collection
stream()
    .flatMap(e -> e.entrySet().stream())
    .collect(toMap(Entry::getKey, Entry::getValue));

The second category was about regular expressions on the hot path. In a service, the developer had to sanitize incoming request strings by modifying characters that weren’t allowed. The earlier implementation ran a raw regular expression substitution on every request.

      
// Anti-pattern: Dynamic regex evaluation per request
String sanitized = input.replaceAll(”[^a-zA-Z0-9.-]”, “_”);

As you might know, evaluating regular expressions involves parsing and state-machine transitions. This logic on high-volume traffic used 46% of the service’s CPU time.

The agent replaced the regex evaluation with a pre-computed lookup table that checked characters by index. The execution got 22 times faster.

The next category was related to unnecessary object allocation that caused OOM crashes. A service frequently checked whether incoming data payloads contained specific metadata fields. To perform the check, the code was creating a new, heavy HashSet on every incoming call.

However, the underlying data object already had an internal lookup method available. Also, instantiating millions of such objects consumed 47% of the service’s total heap collections.

The agent fixed this issue by removing the redundant object instantiations and modified the code to reuse the cached method.

The next category was around library misuse. For example, the discovery involved metric telemetry instrumentation. One of the services tracked operations by looking up a counter from a metric registry on every single call.

      
// Anti-pattern: Looking up metric instances on every function execution
Metrics.counter(”request.count”).increment();

When the query was sent to the registry, it needed dictionary lookups and internal synchronization locks. The profiler showed that the work consumed 66% of the CPU, whereas the actual business logic used only 0.3%.

The agent fixed it by caching the metric counter reference at the time of class initialization. Also, it found that the same issue was happening across three independent services.

Safety, Verification, and Trust Architecture

If you have an AI agent that can optimize code, it’s quite dangerous if the changes are applied without automatic verification. If the agent makes a change that breaks business logic, it’s worse than inefficient code.

To prevent regressions, the agentic pipeline uses the standard SDLC.

In stage 1, you verify the logic. Before you move any code, the agent’s branch must pass all existing unit, integration, and contract tests. This is to make sure that the changes made by the change don’t alter basic inputs, outputs, or handling of edge cases.

In stage 2, you have the canary deployment. If the tests pass, the pipeline spins up a canary deployment in production. The canary instance gets a portion of the traffic. It runs side-by-side with an identical baseline instance that runs the original code.

Stage 3 is about generating the observability report. The platform collects hard telemetry metrics over a big enough window. Some metrics are relative CPU utilization, median latency, P99 latency, and memory allocation rates. They also don’t use any AI model to check the canary results.

In stage 4, you have the final engineering decision. When the canary version shows a good level of performance improvement with zero increase in error rates, the system opens a PR. This PR goes for human review. It includes the code change, the original flame graph, and the canary report. The final decision on deploying the change to production is taken by the human developer.

Shifting Left

Automated production profiling is quite effective. But if you just rely on it, you end up exposing several limitations.

By the time an agent finds an anti-pattern in production, you’ve already paid for days or weeks of wasted compute capacity.

Second, developers are anyway cautious about changing a running service. If you have a service that handles production traffic without crashing, the developers hesitate to just make changes for the sake of optimization.

Lastly, multiple teams often make the exact same mistakes when it comes to patterns. If you run a super-expensive agent on 10 different services just to find the same problem, it’s not very efficient.

These limitations led to Netflix making the decision to shift performance checks left into the early development cycle. Also, they wanted the agents to share their findings across the entire engineering organization.

However, as you might know, language models are stateless. Every time you send a prompt to an LLM, it starts with a clean slate. It might no retain any memory of the bug it found some time back in another service. The Netflix engineering team built a Pattern Catalog to make the models achieve persistence. This was done by pairing a stateless LLM with a stateful catalog. Or a shared memory across the fleet.

The Pattern Catalog was built around 4 key principles.

  • First, it has to be centralized and serve as the single source of truth for all engineering teams. This way, no two teams end up debugging the same issues.

  • The second principle is that the same catalog entries should work across distinct environments. For example, offline profiling, CI/CD pull request checks, and local development tools.

  • Third, you need to format entries so that an automation script can easily inject them into an LLM’s system prompt.

  • Lastly, the contents of the catalog should be reviewable by human developers.

To implement the Pattern Catalog, the Netflix engineering team used a simple Git repository filled with plain Markdown files. They didn’t use vector databases or complex knowledge stores. The idea was borrowed from the “LLM-wiki” concept popularized by Andrej Karpathy.

By using a standard Git repository, the developers got several advantages. For one, developers can diff changes, open pull requests, and use git features to find out why an entry was created. It also scales well to 100s of detailed performance rules without the need for complex search infrastructure. Lastly, plain Markdown is easy for both humans and language models to read without translation layers.

How Netflix Catches Problems Early

With the Pattern Catalog in place, Netflix can handle performance engineering via two paths. Reactive and Proactive.

In the reactive path, your system profiles production services on a recurring schedule or on demand. When the agent finds a new bottleneck, it tests the fix on a canary instance. If everything goes fine, the patch is merged, and the agent documents the new finding in the Pattern Catalog.

In the proactive path, the process starts when a developer creates a new PR. CI tooling performs a fast regex or symbol match against the Pattern Catalog index. If the code in the PR matches known anti-patterns, the CI bot calls an LLM and provides it with the pull request diff. The LLM checks the context and leaves an inline comment that explains the inefficiency. It shows the resource impact and suggests a fix. All this happens before the code ever merges to the main branch.

Conclusion

The key learning from the Netflix engineering experience is that automating performance engineering work is not an all-or-nothing game. You can have organizations adopt workflows along a four-level maturity spectrum.

Level 0 is the manual situation. This is the level where machine learning is not used. Human developers manually capture traces, interpret flame graphs, and trace code paths.

Level 1 is the assist approach. This is the entry point for AI adoption. The LLM acts as an analytical copilot. A developer initiates the profiling process. But they don’t spend time studying flame graphs. Instead, they feed the stack dump to the model. The model finds the hot execution path.

Level 2 is the orchestration level. This is the current state at Netflix. A lot of proactive scanning happens. Also, they use the Pattern Catalog.

Level 3 is the fully autonomous level. This is the long-term vision at Netflix for performance agents. At Level 3, the agents will create their own optimization strategies. They will explore multiple alternative implementations. Or run automated benchmarks.

entries.title: How Nvidia's New Nemotron Model Works
entries.summary: In this article, we’ll look at how Nemotron works and the various techniques used by Nvidia while building it.
entries.content:
Shared Integrations Shouldn’t Need Per-User Tokens (Sponsored)

Some integrations belong to the whole company: a shared Slack bot, a team analytics API key, a server-to-server credential. Asking every user to connect their own account means duplicate tokens, half-finished setups, and a new support ticket every time someone joins.

WorkOS Pipes handles OAuth and token storage so your product can connect to 300+ integrations. With Connection Sharing, an org admin connects a provider once from the drop-in Pipes Admin widget, and every active member can use it right away. The credential is stored against the organization and never sent to the browser.

Nemotron is a family of large language models (LLMs) by Nvidia.

The Nvidia engineering team has built Nemotron with a central design idea. This idea is to build a great language model with good capacity while bringing down the computation and memory requirements. To achieve this, they combine different types of neural-network layers. They use only some parameters per token. Lastly, they also optimize how the model generates answers.

In this article, we’ll look at how Nemotron works and the various techniques used by Nvidia while building it. Here’s what we will cover:

  • How Nemotron generates text

  • How a transformer model spends resources

  • How Nvidia’s Nemotron reduces costs

  • How Nemotron uses Mamba and MoE

  • How Nvidia trains its model

  • How Nvidia uses multi-token prediction

  • How Nvidia reduces storage for models

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

How Nemotron Generates Text

Nemotron is a transformer-based LLM. Therefore, you can expect it to work pretty much the same way as any other LLM.

In a typical LLM, you have some input text that the user sends to the model. This text is divided into tokens. These tokens can be words, parts of words, punctuation, or other text fragments. While processing, the model converts each token into a numerical representation known as an embedding. Next, you have the model process these embeddings through a sequence of layers.

At output time, the model calculates scores for the possible next tokens as part of the decoding process. The decoding step picks a token and appends it to the sequence. Then, it continues generating further tokens. For these calculations, the model makes use of its parameters or weights. The parameters it has learned during the training phase.

Nemotron’s main goal is to make this process of generating text as efficient as possible. This efficiency is critical for AI agents. This is because AI agents repeatedly read instructions, make calls to tools, get responses from those tools, and decide what to do next. You can see that a coding agent might have to make dozens of model calls while trying to solve a problem. Good efficiency can do wonders for such an agent.

Nemotron Lightning model, which has a total of 30 billion parameters, tries to optimize this repeated execution work.

How Does a Transformer Model Spend Resources

A transformer-based language model spends resources on attention and feed-forward computation.

As you already know, the model breaks text into small pieces called tokens. It then converts each token into a list of numbers. You can think of this list as a token’s representation. These numbers change as the model processes the text. It gets to know more about the token and its context. So in a way, the representation of the token changes.

Attention lets you move information between tokens. For example, let’s say you have a sentence “Adam puts the ice cream in the freezer because it was melting”. To interpret “it”, the model has to know about the “ice cream” that was used earlier in the sentence. Attention provides a way to bring that earlier information into the representation of the word “it”.

To understand how this information gathering works, you need to know about three terms: query, key, and value.

A query is the information that a user wants to know about. A key describes what a particular note might be about. A value contains the actual information that the note can provide. The model compares a query with the available keys. It then combines the values and gives more weight to stronger matches. All of these are numerical calculations.

Multiple attention heads perform several such calculations in parallel. Each head learns a different way to match and combine information. Ultimately, the feed-forward network processes the information present at each position. It applies matrix operations and executes nonlinear functions to generate another representation. For example, after attention brings the information about “ice cream” into the representation of “it”, feed-forward computation can refine that representation using patterns learned during training.

You can think of attention as collecting all the useful notes from various places. On the other hand, feed-forward works on the notes that you’ve collected during attention.

Let’s now look at the cost part.

As you might already know, a model generates an answer one token at a time. It produces a token, uses that token as part of the input for the next step, and continues. This is known as autoregressive generation. Much of the text remains the same across each of these steps. However, if you recalculate the keys and values every time, you are repeating a lot of work. The KV cache stores repeated work so that the model can reuse it. But cached work still occupies memory. In full attention, a long history means more keys and values to store. Also, more information needs to be checked at each step.

There is also a cost difference between reading the initial prompt and continuing the answer. For example, when you process a complete prompt, the model has to calculate relationships across many token positions. In a model that looks backward, the first token has one position to consider. The second token has two. The third has three. And so on. These comparisons pile up across the entire prompt.

From this, you can easily guess that if you double a prompt, you need to have four times as much attention comparison work. There is quadratic growth. With KV cache, the earlier information is already prepared, so doubling the history means doubling the attention work. This is linear growth.

How Nvidia’s Nemotron Reduces Costs

Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 model uses Mamba layers and a mixture of experts to reduce costs.

A Mamba layer maintains a compact numerical state. As tokens arrive, this state is kept updated. You can think of it like a running set of notes about what has been read. The state is made up of numerical features learned during training. You can use it to carry information across a long sequence. However, the state doesn’t grow by storing a separate key-value record for every earlier token.

During generation, a Mamba layer’s state size and per-token update cost stay fixed. You can keep updating the model without making the layer search an ever-expanding cache. With a fixed state, you also have one trade-off. Compressing a long history into a bounded representation can make it difficult to retrieve content in a precise manner.

A MoE architecture changes the feed-forward computation. In this setup, your model has many feed-forward networks called experts. A router selects a group of experts to process each token. The model might have a large amount of capacity. But only part of that capacity is used for each token.

How Nemotron Uses Mamba and MoE

Nemotron combines Mamba and attention within one network.

Mamba lets you process sequences in an efficient way. Attention gives direct access to representations associated with earlier positions. Nemotron interleaves these mechanisms so that information can pass through both as it moves through the network.

The layer sequence is defined by the architecture. Every token representation proceeds through that sequence. It encounters Mamba, attention, and expert transformations at their specific positions. Therefore, the attention layer runs on representations that earlier layers have already processed. This way, much of the sequence processing uses a compact state. Selected layers can retain attention’s ability to connect distant positions. The remaining attention layers maintain KV caches.

Mixture of experts (MoE) gives the model capacity without activating every expert. In a dense model, every token goes through the same feed-forward network as every other token at that layer. With MoE, one layer contains many alternative feed-forward networks. A router selects which set of networks is used. The selected experts process the representation. Their output are combined using routing weights.

Nvidia’s Lightning configuration talks about 128 routed experts per MoE layer. 6 experts are selected for each token. This is how a model that has roughly 30 billion parameters but use only roughly 3 billion for a particular token.

Of course, the unused experts are still part of the model. They must remain accessible for later tokens. With sparse activation, you reduce the work done per token. But the total parameter count still impacts the memory needed to host the model.

Lightning also specifies 32 query heads and only 2 key-value heads when it comes to attention. This is a classic grouped-query attention arrangement.

In a basic multi-head attention, each attention head has its own keys and values. With grouped-query attention, you can have several query heads share key-value representations. The model retains multiple ways of querying the context while it stores fewer distinct key-value representations.

How Nvidia Trains Their Models

With training, you first build a language model. Next, you teach it useful behavior. Training determines the values of its weights and the capabilities those calculations can support.

The first stage is pretraining. In this stage, you make the model learn from large quantities of text by predicting tokens and adjusting its weights to reduce prediction errors. By going through many examples, you can build representations of language, code, facts, and other patterns. Lightning’s base model is trained on crawled and synthetic material that covers code, maths, science, and general knowledge.

Nvidia’s pretraining tries to progress the model from a broad data mixture toward more emphasis on high-quality material. The greater breadth of content completes coverage. Later sampling places more weight on selected capabilities.

The next training phase is supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In this training, you teach the model using examples of desired behavior. You can include instructions, conversations, code, tool interactions, and structured responses.

In Nvidia’s SFT recipe, user and system messages provide context. But the training objective is calculated on assistant tokens. Therefore, the model learns which responses should be produced for a specific conversation. If you have a task that needs structured output, the desired response can provide an example of the correct information and the required JSON format.

Reinforcement learning adds feedback to the model’s own attempts. Lightning uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The model generates several responses to a prompt. Those responses receive rewards. The training procedure compares their relative performance to update the model.

The complete training recipe includes an environment that evaluates mathematical answers, executes code against tests, checks instruction compliance, and validates output schemas.

As you can see, there is a logical progression in the training stages. Pretraining helps develop broad predictive capabilities. SFT provides examples of useful behavior. Reinforcement learning refines behavior using feedback on generated attempts.

How Nvidia Uses Multi-Token Prediction

Even if you make each token cheaper, ordinary generation can’t proceed sequentially. The next token depends on the preceding sequence, including tokens that have just been generated.

Multi-token prediction (MTP) trains an auxiliary mechanism to predict further ahead. At inference time, these predictions can support speculative decoding. In this approach, you have a lightweight drafting mechanism that proposes several candidate tokens. The main model evaluates the proposed continuation in a verification pass.

When you accept several proposed tokens, you can have token generation advance by several positions while needing fewer sequential passes through the main model. If you reject a proposal, generation continues from the accepted prefix.

Nvidia’s models ship with integrated MTP capabilities and separate draft models.

How Nvidia Uses Low-Precision Numbers to Reduce Storage

Nvidia also made another optimization regarding how the numbers involved in the calculations are represented.

A BF16 weight uses 16 bits. If you represent the weights with fewer bits, you can reduce the storage requirements. Also, reduce the amount of data transferred through memory. The challenge is approximation error because a smaller set of numbers cannot reproduce every original weight in an exact manner.

Nvidia uses the NVFP4 format. It combines four-bit floating-point values with scaling information. Groups of 16 values share an FP8 scale, with an additional scale at the tensor level. Nvidia also uses quantization-aware distillation (QAD). In QAD, you first create a quantized student model from a BF16 model. The BF16 model remains fixed as the teacher. The student trains with simulated quantization and learns to bring its output scores closer to the teacher’s scores.

Nvidia was able to reduce the size of the model from approx. 66 GB for BF16 to approx. 22 GB for the NVFP4 checkpoint.

Conclusion

Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Super has approx. 120 billion total parameters and 12 billion active parameters. With Ultra, they have scaled this figure to 550 billion total and 55 billion active. Both models use the hybrid Mamba-attention design and introduce LatentMoE.

LatentMoE addresses another cost of expert processing.

The movement of wide token representations and loading expert weights can be quite expensive. The solution is to project the representation into a smaller space for the routed expert computation. Experts process this compact representation. Their outputs are combined, and the result is projected back to the main model dimension. If you reduce the width of the routed computation, you can save memory traffic and communication. Nvidia uses those savings to support more experts and more active expert combinations at a similar inference budget.

The Ultra model also adds a new training technique called multi-teacher on-policy distillation. The model generates its own attempts and receives guidance from multiple domain-specialized teacher models. “On-policy” means learning from attempts generated by the current student. This lets the teacher models guide situations that the student model actually encounters.

AI Terms You Need to Know

Agentic AI: It's an AI system that describes the behavior of the whole system. The agent understands and interprets the goal. It creates a plan and calls tools and APIs to get the results. The agent evaluates the results and corrects the mistakes. It keeps on improving the results until it achieves the desired goal.

Large Reasoning Model: It’s a type of model that is trained to solve problems which require lots of logical steps. It breaks a problem into smaller problems and performs reasoning on them to come up with the right answer.

Vector Database: It's a type of database that stores vectors, as the name implies. These vectors are actually lists of numbers which represent the meaning and characteristics of text, audio, video or other data.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG): It's a technique to provide relevant information to the model when needed. The relevant information is mostly stored in a vector database, but retrieval can also be through APIs, SQL, or hybrid search.

Model Context Protocol (MCP): It provides a standard interface to AI applications to connect and access external tools and APIs. The communication happens through the MCP client within the AI applications communicating through MCP servers.

GPT-2 to GPT-6: What Actually Changed

It's been seven years from GPT-2 to GPT-6, and a lot has changed.

The diagram below shows each generation and its key highlights, based on the public information we know.

GPT-2 (2019): More like a prototype to validate the potential of the decoder-only transformer. This was a 1.5B-parameter model that only went through pre-training with next-token prediction. The trained model was only capable of continuing text, not answering questions.

GPT-3 (2020): The same recipe as GPT-2, just much bigger and trained on more data to test how far scale alone could go. GPT-3 had 175B parameters, more than 100 times the size of GPT-2, and still only went through pre-training. The scale allowed it to show in-context learning capabilities. When shown some examples, the model could follow them.

GPT-4 (2023): On top of pre-training, OpenAI fine-tuned it with RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback), so it was not just a completion model but could actually answer questions. It was also multimodal, meaning that it could process input images as well as text, and it handled up to 32K tokens of context.

GPT-5 (2025): The first GPT generation with built-in reasoning. Given a prompt, tools, and an effort level, the trained model could generate reasoning tokens before the answer. Its context window grew to 400K tokens, with a router in ChatGPT to decide when a prompt needed thinking mode.

GPT-6 (2026): This new model has a bigger context window (1.05M), supports async tool calling, and is generally safer. An interesting feature, called mid-turn steering, is that it can take a new instruction while it's thinking.

Al Topics to Learn before Taking Al/ML Interviews

AI interviews often test fundamentals, not tools. This visual splits them into two buckets that show up repeatedly: Traditional AI and Modern AI.

Traditional AI focuses on fundamental ML topics, mostly from before neural networks became dominant.

Modern AI focuses on neural network foundations and newer concepts like transformers, RAG, and post-training.

Interviewers generally expect you to know both. They expect you to explain how they work, when they break, and the trade-offs.

Use this as a checklist, and make sure you can explain each topic clearly before your next AI interview.

Over to you: which topic here do you find hardest to explain under interview pressure? What else is missing?

How GPUs Work at a High Level

When people say GPUs are powerful, what they really mean is this: GPUs are built for massive parallelism from the ground up.

Let’s break down what’s happening under the hood.

At the top level, a GPU chip is made up of many Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs). Think of SMs as mini parallel engines replicated across the chip. Instead of one big brain, you get dozens of smaller ones working simultaneously.

Inside each SM:

  • A Warp Scheduler decides which group of threads (a warp) runs next.

  • Dozens of CUDA Cores execute instructions in parallel.

  • A Register File stores thread-local data at ultra-low latency.

  • Load/Store units move data between registers and memory.

  • Texture units handle specialized memory operations.

  • L1 Cache provides fast, on-SM data access.

Each SM works independently, but they’re connected through an on-chip interconnect. Below that sits the L2 Cache, shared across all SMs. This is the coordination layer. If one SM misses in L1, it checks L2 before going to global memory.

Then come the Memory Controllers, which interface with Global Memory. This is where things get interesting:

  • Extremely high bandwidth

  • Much higher latency than on-chip memory

That’s why GPUs rely on massive parallelism. While some threads wait on memory, thousands of others keep executing.

entries.title: Data Movement Strategies In System Design
entries.summary: To manage this movement of data, you need to make decisions about when and how information should travel within a system and outside it.
entries.content:
Software systems don’t keep information in one place all the time. When a user makes a request to the system, it goes from the application to a server. A database might store the records needed to process it. Also, other components may need to know about any changes.

You need to move data to connect all these separate activities so that they can work as a coherent system.

To manage this movement of data, you need to make decisions about when and how information should travel within a system and outside it. This is where you have multiple strategies that can be used to handle data movement. In this article, we’ll look at the key strategies of data movement along with their benefits. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The source, consumer, and trigger of data movement

  • What is the pull approach

  • The polling approach

  • The push approach

  • The long polling approach

  • Continuous communication with SSE and WebSockets

  • The role of message queues

  • Change data capture for database changes

  • How to choose a data movement strategy
